solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Dump plate if damaged

indicators.note: something damaged has been knocked out of shape, so the letters lose their original order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone advises throwing out a crockery plate once it is chipped or broken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dump' looks like an instruction to throw away, but it is a noun meaning a shabby place. A FLEAPIT is British slang for a run-down old cinema.
explanation.definitionFit: A fleapit is a grubby, run-down cinema or theatre, and a dump is any squalid, neglected building.

clue.text: Half a bone is replaced in hip

indicators.note: when things are replaced they are put back in different positions, so the letters get a new order

blocks.note: all eleven letters of the phrase, taken as written

explanation.surface: A surgeon describes a hip operation in which part of a bone is swapped for an implant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half' tempts you to take half of 'bone', but the whole phrase is the fodder. 'Hip' is the trendy adjective, not the joint.
explanation.definitionFit: Hip is slang for trendy, being up to date with the latest styles and tastes.

clue.text: Always best avoiding peak — this the highest!

indicators.note: a down word's peak is its top letter, and avoiding it means leaving that letter out

blocks.note: ever means always, as in 'ever hopeful'
taken as written before losing its top letter

explanation.surface: A climber is told it is always wiser to skip a summit, yet this one is the highest of all.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue the 'peak' of BEST is its first letter, B, leaving EST. 'Peak' also teases the answer, a mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: Mount Everest in the Himalayas is the tallest mountain on Earth, its summit standing above every other.

clue.text: Man, upset male in bits

indicators.note: to upset something is to knock it over, so its letters fall into a different order

blocks.note: a chessman or draughtsman is a piece
taken as written

explanation.surface: A distressed man has gone to pieces emotionally.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man' reads as a person, but it is a playing piece in chess or draughts.
explanation.definitionFit: Piecemeal describes something done gradually, a portion at a time, rather than all at once.

clue.text: Touring company moved to Peru

indicators.note: things that are moved end up in new places, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A travelling business relocates to South America.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Company' suggests a firm, but here it is a group of performers.
explanation.definitionFit: A troupe is a group of actors, dancers or entertainers who often travel around giving performances.

clue.text: Call on grandma, mum and uncle last of all

indicators.note: the final letter of each of the words listed is the one taken

blocks.note: closing letters of on, grandma, mum, uncle; 'and' is just a joiner

explanation.surface: Someone plans to visit grandma and mum, leaving their uncle until the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Call on' reads as a phrase meaning visit, but 'Call' alone is the definition and 'on' begins the list of words.
explanation.definitionFit: To call someone something is to give them a title or label, exactly as naming does.

clue.text: Head: might that be screwed on?

blocks.note: first meaning: slang for the head
second meaning: a small metal piece turned onto a bolt

explanation.walkthrough: The surface recalls having your head screwed on, meaning being sensible; the second meaning is the hardware fixed onto a bolt.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is informal slang for a person's skull, and also names the threaded fastener twisted onto a bolt.

clue.text: Old pollsters welcoming a NZ native

indicators.note: to welcome a guest is to take them inside, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: MORI was a British opinion-polling firm, now merged into Ipsos
taken as written

explanation.surface: Former opinion researchers greet someone from New Zealand.
explanation.walkthrough: MORI (Market and Opinion Research International) was a well-known British polling company; 'Old' reflects that it is now part of Ipsos.
explanation.definitionFit: The Maori are the indigenous Polynesian people of New Zealand, living there before European settlement.

clue.text: Landscape viewed, reportedly

indicators.note: what is reported is passed on by word of mouth, so we go by how the word sounds

blocks.note: seen means viewed

explanation.surface: A landscape is described as having been looked at, according to reports.
explanation.walkthrough: SEEN and SCENE are pronounced the same in standard English.
explanation.definitionFit: A scene can be a view or vista spread out before an observer, like a painted landscape.

clue.text: Published letters for remote district

blocks.note: a book that is out has been published
post is the mail delivered

explanation.surface: Mail is printed and distributed for people in a far-flung area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Published letters' reads as one idea, such as an edition of correspondence, but splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An outpost is a small settlement or station far from the centre, at the edge of territory.

clue.text: Traitorous motive in board

indicators.note: something placed in another thing sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a motive is a reason for acting
a board can be a table, as in 'board and lodging'

explanation.surface: A member of a company board harbours a treacherous motive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Board' looks like a company's directors, but it is a table, as in bed and board.
explanation.definitionFit: Treasonable acts betray one's country or sovereign, which is what a traitor does.

clue.text: Something frozen that is keeping cold

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold onto it, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: i.e. is the abbreviation for 'that is' (Latin id est)
C stands for cold, as on taps

explanation.surface: A frozen item keeps things cold, like an ice pack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeping cold' reads as preserving food, but 'keeping' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Water turns solid when chilled below zero degrees, and that solid is exactly what freezing produces.

clue.text: Even six pence extremely bad — too much money

definitions.note: a phrase describing cost, standing for an adjective

indicators.note: the extremes of a word are its two ends, so only its outer letters are kept
something gone bad is spoilt and disordered, so these letters are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
first and last letters of pence

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles that even sixpence is far too high a price.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Even' looks like an adverb for emphasis, but it is part of the fodder. Sixpence was an old British coin worth half a shilling.
explanation.definitionFit: Something expensive costs a lot, more than the buyer thinks reasonable to pay.

clue.text: Calf, quite possibly, in US state?

blocks.note: first meaning: a recently born animal of a Channel Island dairy breed
second meaning: the state on the east coast between New York and Pennsylvania

explanation.walkthrough: A Jersey is a breed of dairy cow from the Channel Island of Jersey, so a newborn calf of that breed is, playfully, a new Jersey.
explanation.definitionFit: New Jersey is one of the original thirteen American states, and a young Jersey cow is newly born.

clue.text: In quarantine, the risk lower …

indicators.note: the answer is found inside the words that follow, running across them

blocks.note: the end of quarantine, all of the, and the start of risk

explanation.surface: Health officials note that keeping people in quarantine reduces the danger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lower' looks like a verb meaning reduce, but it is the adjective; the ellipsis links to the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Nether is an old-fashioned adjective for something situated beneath, as in the nether regions.

clue.text: … lowest, possibly, for young birds

indicators.note: 'possibly' offers one of the possible arrangements of the letters rather than the given one

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue, the danger is lowest perhaps for fledglings.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis makes 'lowest' seem to continue 'lower' from the clue before, but here it is just the letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: Owlets are baby owls, the chicks of that nocturnal bird of prey.

clue.text: 19 across rough game with Rob

indicators.note: rough means crude and unpolished, so the letters come out in a disorderly arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A violent match is played alongside someone named Rob.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer to 19 across is BAN, which is the definition here; 'Rob' looks like a verb or a name but is plain fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: An embargo is an official prohibition, especially on trade with a particular country, so it is a ban.

clue.text: Understand imperial measure

blocks.note: first meaning: to grasp or work out
second meaning: a unit of depth equal to six feet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Imperial' refers to the old British system of units; this one is used for the depth of water.
explanation.definitionFit: To get to the bottom of a problem is to comprehend it, and the same word names six feet of water depth.

clue.text: Text lab put out about each old weapon

indicators.note: something put out is disturbed or displaced, so the letters are rearranged
about means around, so one piece surrounds the other

blocks.note: taken as written
ea. is the abbreviation for each

explanation.surface: A text from the laboratory, released to the public, discusses every historical weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put out' reads as publish, but it signals rearrangement. The answer is also slang for a domineering older woman.
explanation.definitionFit: A battle-axe is a broad-bladed axe once used in warfare, a weapon from earlier centuries.

clue.text: On having departed this evening, stretched

indicators.note: once something has departed it is no longer present, so those letters are taken away

blocks.note: this evening is tonight
taken as written, the part that goes

explanation.surface: Having left this evening, someone is stretched thin.
explanation.walkthrough: Removing the inner ON from TONIGHT leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A rope pulled taut is stretched, with no slack left in it.

clue.text: Located in suburb, a new block

indicators.note: the answer is found within the run of words that follows

blocks.note: the last letter of suburb, all of a, the first of new

explanation.surface: A fresh housing block is located in a suburb.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Block' looks like a building, but it is the verb meaning prohibit.
explanation.definitionFit: To ban something is to forbid it, stopping it from happening, so it is to prevent or obstruct.

clue.text: Single frightfully hot tongue

indicators.note: 'frightfully' suggests something terribly done, so the letters are thrown into disarray

blocks.note: taken as written
H stands for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: One terribly spicy tongue, perhaps a dish on a menu.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tongue' suggests the organ or a meat, but it means language.
explanation.definitionFit: Tongue is an old word for a language, and English is one of the world's most spoken languages.

clue.text: British leader I sent up, little rascal

indicators.note: in a down answer, sending something up makes it read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the Prime Minister, Britain's head of government
taken as written

explanation.surface: A British leader confesses to being mocked as a cheeky little rogue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sent up' looks like mocking, as in a send-up, but in a down clue it turns the letters upward.
explanation.definitionFit: An imp is a small mischievous sprite, and the word is used for a naughty child.

clue.text: Woody plant right inside untidy bush

indicators.note: an untidy arrangement is a messy one, so the letters are jumbled
a piece placed inside sits within another piece

blocks.note: R is the abbreviation for right
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woody plant sits right in the middle of an overgrown bush.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush' seems to be the definition next to 'plant', but it is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A shrub is a small woody-stemmed plant with several branches growing near the ground.

clue.text: Close ranks to preserve banks!

indicators.note: to bank something is to deposit and hold it, so the preceding words hold the answer

blocks.note: the end of ranks, all of to, and the start of preserve

explanation.surface: A rallying cry to unite and defend the riverbanks or the banks of the financial system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close ranks' looks like one phrase, but 'Close' alone is the definition, a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To close a shop or a meeting is to bring it to an end, halting it.

clue.text: Tree, European fixture at spring festival?

blocks.note: may is another name for the hawthorn
a Pole is a person from Poland

explanation.surface: A tree and a European feature at a springtime celebration.
explanation.walkthrough: May is the hawthorn, which blossoms in May; the question mark flags a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A maypole is a tall decorated post that dancers circle with ribbons at May Day celebrations.
